section_summaries.epidemiology: Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading infectious cause of death among adults and the primary killer of people with HIV, largely affecting low- to middle-income countries. About 2 billion people, or one-third of the world's population, have Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. In 2016, 6.34 million new TB cases were reported globally, with Southeast Asia (42%), Western Pacific (26%), and sub-Saharan Africa (20%) being high-burden regions. High incidence rates are often linked to TB/HIV co-infection, with approximately 75% of HIV co-infected TB patients living in sub-Saharan Africa. The rise in multi-drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB, resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin) and rifampin-resistant TB is a concerning trend, associated with lower cure rates. Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is also reported, though its epidemiology is underestimated due to limited testing access. Roughly 1 million children develop TB annually, often under-diagnosed and under-treated. Infants and young children are at higher risk of severe disease, especially with immunodeficiency or malnutrition.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: TB is an airborne pathogen, transmitted via aerosolized droplet nuclei (1–5 µm) from an infectious host. Bacilli-containing droplets remain airborne for hours to days and are small enough to be inhaled into the terminal alveoli. After inhalation, bacilli may extend via lung lymphatics to other areas of the lungs and to other organs throughout the body. Cellular immunity develops approximately 6 to 12 weeks later, leading to eradication of bacilli or granuloma formation at infection sites. This cellular immunity is the basis for the tuberculin skin test (TST) and prevents progression to symptomatic disease in most infected individuals who are considered to have latent infection. However, approximately 10% of infected individuals will develop active disease: in the acute setting (primary TB, within 1-2 years of infection) or as reactivation TB (more than 2 years after infection), which occurs in approximately 5% to 10% of infected individuals over their lifetime. HIV infection increases this risk to approximately 5% to 10% per year. Without anti-TB chemotherapy, approximately 50% of patients with active disease die within 5 years, 30% recover spontaneously, and 20% remain infectious.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: The diverse clinical presentations of TB result from the bacilli's ability to infect virtually any organ. Approximately 70% to 90% of active cases involve the lung, while 10% to 30% are extra-pulmonary, with up to 15% having both. Extra-pulmonary involvement is more common in immunocompromised individuals (e.g., up to 70% of AIDS patients) and children. Active TB manifestations are often sub-acute or chronic, developing over weeks to months, and include constitutional symptoms like fever, night sweats, anorexia, and weight loss. Immunosuppressed individuals may present with attenuated or absent signs. Pulmonary TB commonly presents with lower lobe infiltrates and/or hilar adenopathy in primary TB. Reactivation TB typically involves upper lobe cavities, fibrosis, and mediastinal retraction. Cavitary lesions are often associated with hemoptysis. Extra-pulmonary TB includes tuberculous adenitis (most common, often cervical lymphadenopathy/scrofula), pleural tuberculosis (pleural effusions), Central Nervous System (CNS) TB (mass lesions or meningoencephalitis with neurological deficits, seizures, fever, headache, nuchal rigidity), osteoarticular TB (frequently involving the spine, Pott's disease, with chronic back pain, deformities, or arthritis), and other manifestations like gastrointestinal TB, genitourinary TB, cutaneous TB, pericarditis, larynx, adrenal glands, and eye involvement. Disseminated TB may show a miliary pattern on chest radiographs.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Accurate TB diagnosis remains a serious challenge; smear-negative pulmonary TB and extra-pulmonary TB are predominantly clinical diagnoses. Confirmation is particularly difficult in immunocompromised individuals and children, often necessitating a clinical diagnosis and empiric treatment. Novel diagnostic methods include: Genotypic Testing, with Xpert MTB/RIF (GeneXpert) recommended as the primary diagnostic test for all persons with possible TB. It detects M. tuberculosis DNA and rifampin resistance, producing rapid results (2 hours). Other genotypic tests, like molecular line probe assays, identify TB and resistance to multiple drugs. Sputum Smear Microscopy is often available in resource-limited settings but is not recommended as the initial diagnostic test for TB due to its insensitivity, though it's useful for monitoring treatment. Tuberculosis Culture is considered the 'gold standard' but can miss cases and is slow (6-8 weeks for solid culture; 8-16 days for liquid media). Culture allows for Drug Susceptibility Tests (DST), crucial for designing regimens in MDR-TB areas. Radiography (chest x-ray) is commonly used, but findings can mimic other pulmonary diseases; atypical presentations (miliary, intra-thoracic adenopathy, pleural effusions) are common in HIV-positive patients, where chest radiographs may even be normal. CT and ultrasound are useful for suspected extra-pulmonary TB. For extra-pulmonary TB, relevant samples (pleural fluid, CSF, ascetic fluid, lymph node aspirate/biopsy, blood, urine) should be obtained for Xpert MTB/RIF and TB culture, despite often low bacillary loads. Tests for Tuberculosis Infection include Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA), but neither distinguishes latent from active infection. Pediatric TB diagnosis is challenging due to lower bacillary load, difficult specimen collection, and common extra-pulmonary disease, often requiring empirical treatment. Xpert MTB/RIF is recommended as the primary diagnostic test for children.
section_summaries.treatment: Tuberculosis treatment requires combination therapy to avoid drug-resistant pathogens. Novel therapeutic agents and regimens are being tested and implemented, though access remains a challenge. Empiric TB treatment is often necessary for smear-negative or difficult-to-confirm TB, especially in clinically unstable or HIV-positive patients. For drug-susceptible TB, standard first-line (Category I) treatment involves an intensive phase with at least four anti-tuberculous drugs daily, followed by a continuation phase with fewer drugs. WHO guidelines emphasize daily treatment for 6 months, prompt initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV co-infection, use of fixed-dose combination tablets, and community-based adherence support. TB meningitis and osteoarticular TB require 12 months of treatment. Treatment response monitoring includes observing rapid improvement in constitutional symptoms and sputum conversion to negative. Failure to respond by the second month triggers re-evaluation for adherence issues or drug-resistant TB. Paradoxical worsening (immune reconstitution syndrome), especially in HIV-positive patients on ART, may be managed with corticosteroids. For drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB, XDR-TB), individuals with rifampin resistance should undergo drug resistance testing and be treated with all-oral regimens, typically including bedaquiline, linezolid, and a third-generation fluoroquinolone, plus clofazimine and cycloserine. Delamanid is an alternative. Injectable agents are generally discouraged. Adjunctive treatments include steroids for meningeal TB and paradoxical worsening, and surgery for localized disease or extensive soft tissue involvement in select cases. Patient adherence is crucial for successful outcomes, supported by education, incentives, case management, and nutritional supplementation.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention strategies for tuberculosis include treating latent TB infection to prevent progression to active disease. Standard preventive therapy is isoniazid 300 mg daily for 6-9 months, effective and not associated with resistance. A 12-week regimen of high-dose isoniazid and rifapentine once a week can also improve completion rates. For latent MDR-TB infection, fluoroquinolone-based therapy has shown efficacy, with experts recommending at least two drugs to which the infecting isolate is susceptible. In children, prevention focuses on rapid diagnosis of adult infection sources, prompt treatment of infected adults, and assessment of household contacts. For children with no active disease, TB infection treatment should be initiated. The Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine, a live attenuated M. bovis vaccine, reduces severe forms of TB (meningitis, disseminated TB) in childhood and is given as a single dose after birth in high TB burden countries. However, its effectiveness decreases over time, and booster doses are not indicated. BCG is contraindicated in HIV-infected children due to the risk of disseminated disease.

tables.title: Overlapping Toxicities of Antiretroviral and Tuberculosis Drugs
rows: Linezolid (Lzd), Cs, H, Aminoglycosides, Eto/Pto, E

Avoid use of D4T, ddI, and ddC in combination with Cs or Lzd because of theoretically increased peripheral neuropathy. If these agents must be used and peripheral neuropathy develops, replace the antiretroviral agent with a less neurotoxic agent.

Efavirenz has a high rate of CNS side effects (confusion, impaired concentration, depersonalization, abnormal dreams, insomnia, and dizziness) in the first 2-3 wk, which typically resolve on their own. If the CNS side effects do not resolve on their own, consider substitution of the agent. At present, there are limited data on the use of EFV with Cs; concurrent use is accepted practice with frequent monitoring for CNS toxicity. Frank psychosis is rare with EFV alone.

Severe depression can be seen in 2.4% of patients receiving EFV*; Consider substituting EFV if severe depression develops. The severe socioeconomic circumstances of many patients with chronic disease can also contribute to depression.

Rule out more serious causes of headache such as bacterial meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, CNS toxoplasmosis, etc. Use of analgesics (ibuprofen, paracetamol) and hydration may help. Headache secondary to AZT, EFV, and Cs is usually self-limited.
Ritonavir (RTV), D4T, nevirapine (NVP), and most others
Eto/Pto, PAS, H, E, Z, and others
Nausea and vomiting are common adverse effects and can be managed. Persistent vomiting and abdominal pain may be a result of developing lactic acidosis and/or hepatitis secondary to medications.
All HAART has been associated with abdominal pain
Abdominal pain is a common adverse effect and often benign; however, abdominal pain may be an early symptom of severe adverse effects such as pancreatitis, hepatitis, or lactic acidosis.

Avoid use of these agents together. If an agent causes pancreatitis, suspend it permanently and do not use any of the pancreatitis-producing anti-HIV medications (D4T, ddI, or ddC) in the future. Also consider gallstones or alcohol as a potential cause of pancreatitis.
Diarrhea is a common adverse effect. Also consider opportunistic infections as a cause of diarrhea or Clostridium difficile (a cause of pseudomembranous colitis).
NVP, EFV, all protease inhibitors (RTV > other protease inhibitors), all nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs)
H, R, E, Z, PAS, Eto/Pto, fluoroquinolones
Also consider TMP/SMX as a cause of hepatotoxicity if the patient is receiving this medication. Also rule out viral etiologies as cause of hepatitis (hepatitis A, B, C, and cytomegalovirus).
Abacavir (ABC), NVP, EFV, D4T, and others
H,R, Z, PAS, fluoroquinolones, and others

Do not re-challenge with ABC (can result in life-threatening anaphylaxis). Do not re-challenge with an agent that caused Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Also consider TMP/SMX as a cause of skin rash if the patient is receiving this medication. Thioacetazone is contraindicated in HIV because of life-threatening rash.
If an agent causes lactic acidosis, replace it with an agent less likely to cause lactic acidosis.

TDF may cause renal injury with the characteristic features of Fanconi's syndrome, hypophosphatemia, hypouricemia, proteinuria, normoglycemic glycosuria, and in some cases acute renal failure. There are no data on the concurrent use of TDF with aminoglycosides or Cm. Use TDF with caution in patients receiving aminoglycosides or Cm. Even without the concurrent use of TDF, HIV-infected patients have an increased risk of renal toxicity secondary to aminoglycosides and Cm. Frequent creatinine and electrolyte monitoring every 1-3 wk is recommended. Many anti-virals and anti-tuberculosis medications need to be dose adjusted for renal insufficiency.

No overlapping toxicities regarding nephrolithiasis have been documented between antiretroviral therapy (ART) and anti-tuberculosis medications. Adequate hydration prevents nephrolithiasis in patients taking IDV. If nephrolithiasis develops while on IDV, substitute with another protease inhibitor if possible.

Diarrhea and/or vomiting can contribute to electrolyte disturbances. Even without the concurrent use of TDF, HIV-infected patients have an increased risk of both renal toxicity and electrolyte disturbances secondary to aminoglycosides and Cm.

Monitor blood counts regularly. Replace AZT if bone marrow suppression develops. Consider suspension of Lzd. Also consider TMP/SMX as a cause if the patient is receiving this medication. Consider adding folinic acid supplements, especially if receiving TMP/SMX.
Suspend agent responsible for optic neuritis permanently and replace with an agent that does not cause optic neuritis.

No overlapping toxicities regarding hyperlipidemia have been documented between ART and anti-tuberculosis medications. Follow World Health Organization (WHO) ART guidelines for management of hyperlipidemia.
No overlapping toxicities regarding lipodystrophy have been documented between ART and anti-tuberculosis medications. Follow WHO ART guidelines for management of lipodystrophy.

Protease inhibitors tend to cause insulin resistance and hyperglycemia. Eto/Pto tend to make insulin control in diabetics more difficult, and can result in hypoglycemia and poor glucose regulation. Gatifloxacin is no longer recommended for use in treatment of TB because of this side effect.

There is potential for overlying toxicity; however, evidence is mixed. Several studies show subclinical hypothyroidism associated with HAART, particularly stavudine. PAS and Eto/Pto, especially in combination, can commonly cause hypothyroidism.
